title: How Hoover Dam Was Built by Jobless Men
hook: In 1931, men collapsing in 120-degree heat had to wall off a wild river with concrete that should have taken a century to cool, and finished two years early.
era: Black Canyon on the Colorado River, 1932
thumbnail_picture: Huge close view on the right of a gray concrete dam wall rising in a deep desert canyon, steam drifting off fresh concrete, a sweating 1930s worker in a cloth cap and overalls on the right staring up at it with wide-eyed shock, orange desert light, the left third of the frame empty sky and rock
description:
How Hoover Dam was built in the Great Depression: the story of the jobless men who tamed the Colorado River in the Nevada desert, the tunnels, the heat, and the concrete that would have taken a century to cool. Hoover Dam history, explained.

Thousands of desperate workers, four giant tunnels, daring high scalers and a clever cooling trick finished the dam about two years early and sent power to Los Angeles and the Southwest.

Sources:
- U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, Hoover Dam History and Construction pages
- Joseph E. Stevens, "Hoover Dam: An American Adventure" (University of Oklahoma Press, 1988)
- Michael Hiltzik, "Colossus: Hoover Dam and the Making of the American Century" (Free Press, 2010)
- National Park Service, Lake Mead National Recreation Area
tags: why hoover dam concrete still cooling

scenes.narration: Summer, 1931. In a Nevada canyon, the air hits a hundred and twenty degrees, and men are collapsing where they stand.
scenes.delivery: low, tense, like the start of a thriller
scenes.caption: THE IMPOSSIBLE POUR
scenes.picture: Close-up of a lean 1930s worker, about 30, short brown hair, dusty overalls, cloth cap, slumped to his knees on cracked red desert ground, drenched in sweat, another worker in overalls gripping his arm to hold him up, blazing white sun and shimmering heat haze, red canyon walls behind.

scenes.narration: But they can't quit. In the Great Depression, this job is all that stands between their families and hunger.
scenes.caption: TWO YEARS EARLY
scenes.picture: A tired 1930s mother in a faded cotton dress and two thin children sitting outside a canvas tent in a dusty desert camp, an empty tin pot beside them, watching a line of workers in overalls walk away toward a canyon, harsh noon light.

scenes.narration: Their task: wall off a wild river with concrete so massive it should take a century to cool. Somehow, they finished two years early.
scenes.delivery: awed, then a curious lift on the last sentence
scenes.caption: THE QUESTION
scenes.picture: A gigantic half-built gray concrete dam wall filling a narrow red rock canyon, a rushing brown river at its foot, three tiny workers in overalls and cloth caps standing in front looking up at it, dusk with a glowing orange sky.

scenes.narration: Go back to 1931. America is broke, and millions of men are standing in line for work that isn't there.
scenes.picture: A long line of thin 1930s men in worn suits and flat caps standing in a dusty city street outside a closed brick factory with dark windows, tired faces, gray sky, Great Depression.

scenes.narration: Then a rumor spreads. So men sell their cars, ride freight trains, and chase it into the Nevada desert.
scenes.caption: CHASING A RUMOR
scenes.picture: Three thin 1930s men in worn clothes with bundles on their backs clinging to the side of an open steam freight train boxcar rolling through the Nevada desert at sunrise, hopeful faces.

scenes.narration: The rumor is true. The government plans a dam in Black Canyon, on the Colorado River.
scenes.caption: BLACK CANYON
scenes.picture: A narrow deep canyon of dark volcanic rock with a muddy brown Colorado River rushing through the bottom, empty and wild, no people, golden morning light, wide shot.

scenes.narration: But the Colorado is wild. Every spring, snowmelt from the Rockies turns it into a flood that wrecks farms downstream.
scenes.caption: A WILD RIVER
scenes.picture: A raging brown flood river bursting over its banks and drowning a small farm, a wooden barn half underwater and flooded fields, dark stormy sky, 1920s desert valley.

scenes.narration: So seven states that argued for years over its water finally strike a deal in 1922, and in 1928 Congress approves one giant dam.
scenes.caption: SEVEN STATES
scenes.picture: Seven men in 1920s suits and hats leaning over a wooden table in an office with a large window, two of them shaking hands across it, relieved smiles, soft afternoon light.

scenes.narration: It will be the tallest dam on Earth, taller than a sixty-story skyscraper.
scenes.caption: 726 FEET TALL
scenes.picture: Dramatic low-angle view looking up at a colossal curved gray concrete dam wall towering over a canyon, tiny workers at its base for scale, deep blue sky.

scenes.narration: But there's a catch. Black Canyon has no town, no shade, and barely a road.
scenes.caption: NOTHING THERE
scenes.picture: A bare dusty desert plain with a single dirt track, cactus and rocks, no buildings and no shade, a lone 1930s pickup truck kicking up a trail of dust under harsh sun.

scenes.narration: So before anyone pours a drop of concrete, they have to build a whole city.
scenes.caption: BOULDER CITY
scenes.picture: Workers in overalls and cloth caps hammering the frame of a new wooden house with a sloped roof on a desert hillside, stacks of lumber beside them, bright day, more half-built houses behind.

scenes.narration: Once word gets out, thousands of men line up for every opening, and every one of them is desperate.
scenes.caption: JOB LINE
scenes.picture: A long line of lean 1930s men in worn work clothes waiting in the desert sun in front of a small wooden hiring shack with an open window, hopeful and anxious faces, dust in the air.

scenes.narration: A hired man earns about four dollars a day. In 1931, that's the difference between eating and not.
scenes.caption: FOUR DOLLARS A DAY
scenes.picture: Close-up of a worker's rough sunburned hands holding a few silver coins above a folded brown paper pay envelope, dusty overalls sleeve, warm light, shallow background.

scenes.narration: But housing isn't ready, so families camp by the river in tents and scrap-wood shacks. They call it Ragtown.
scenes.caption: RAGTOWN
scenes.picture: A shantytown of patched canvas tents and scrap-wood shacks on a dry desert riverbank at dusk, laundry on a line, a 1930s mother in a plain dress and her small child by a cookfire.

scenes.narration: Then summer comes. The thermometer hits a hundred and twenty degrees, and men start collapsing in their bunks.
scenes.caption: SUMMER 1931
scenes.picture: A lean 1930s worker, about 30, short brown hair, slumped sweating on a wooden bunk inside a stifling tin-roof hut, pale exhausted face, a blazing white sun glaring through the window.

scenes.narration: Angry workers walk off the job in August, demanding better pay and safer work. The strike fizzles, but the danger stays.
scenes.caption: THE STRIKE
scenes.picture: Three angry 1930s workers in dusty overalls and cloth caps standing together with arms crossed outside rows of wooden bunkhouses at a desert work camp, heat haze, defiant faces.

scenes.narration: And the first real problem is waiting. You can't build a dam in a river that's still flowing.
scenes.caption: THE PROBLEM
scenes.picture: A clean-shaven 1930s engineer in his 40s, white shirtsleeves and tie, brown felt hat, standing with a worried face beside wooden survey stakes on a bare ledge above a muddy rushing Colorado River in a canyon.

scenes.narration: So the plan is wild: blast four giant tunnels through the canyon walls, and send the whole Colorado around the dam site.
scenes.caption: FOUR TUNNELS
scenes.picture: A huge round tunnel mouth blasted into a canyon wall beside a rushing brown river, small 1930s trucks parked in front of it for scale, dust hanging in the air.

scenes.narration: Each tunnel is fifty-six feet wide, nearly as tall as a five-story building.
scenes.caption: 56 FEET WIDE
scenes.picture: Inside a vast round rock tunnel under construction, a small 1930s dump truck at the center, rough rock walls curving overhead, bright work lamps, very high ceiling.

scenes.narration: So crews drill into solid rock around the clock, and dynamite shakes the canyon day and night.
scenes.caption: DYNAMITE
scenes.picture: A tunnel face where three workers in cloth caps operate heavy drilling rigs on a rock wall, a burst of dust and sparks, dramatic orange lamp light.

scenes.narration: But inside, the tunnels are ovens. Truck exhaust fills the air, and the heat soars past a hundred and twenty degrees.
scenes.caption: OVEN TUNNELS
scenes.picture: Inside a hazy tunnel filled with gray exhaust smoke, a sweating 1930s worker in a cloth cap wiping his face beside an idling truck, orange glow, stifling air.

scenes.narration: Men faint. Men die, officially of heat or pneumonia, though their families blame the fumes.
scenes.caption: THE COST
scenes.picture: Two workers in overalls carrying a limp, exhausted comrade out of a tunnel mouth into daylight, a doctor in a white coat waiting with a worried face, desert canyon behind.

scenes.narration: Still, the work goes on, until the day the river must move. In November 1932, crews dump rock and close off the old channel.
scenes.caption: NOVEMBER 1932
scenes.picture: A line of dump trucks tipping gray rubble from a high canyon ledge into a brown river, dust rising, workers on the bank watching intently, November light.

scenes.narration: The Colorado turns. It plunges into the tunnels, and for the first time the riverbed lies bare.
scenes.caption: RIVER REDIRECTED
scenes.picture: A churning brown river pouring into a giant tunnel mouth in a canyon wall, white spray and mist, the old dry cracked riverbed lying bare beside it.

scenes.narration: Now crews dig down through mud and loose rock until they hit solid bedrock.
scenes.caption: DIGGING TO BEDROCK
scenes.picture: A deep excavated pit at the bottom of a canyon, a steam shovel scraping muddy rock, a few workers with shovels, tall cliffs rising all around, clouds of steam.

scenes.narration: But the canyon walls above are cracked and crumbling. One loose boulder could crush everyone below.
scenes.caption: FALLING ROCK
scenes.picture: A steep cracked canyon wall with a large loose boulder tipping from the edge, tiny workers far below looking up, dust trickling down the rock.

scenes.narration: So the company turns to its boldest men: the high scalers. They hang from ropes, hundreds of feet up.
scenes.caption: HIGH SCALERS
scenes.picture: A lone 1930s high scaler in a hardened cloth cap dangling on a rope against a towering sheer canyon cliff, drill in hand, the tiny river far below.

scenes.narration: Swinging in the wind, they pry off boulders and drill holes for dynamite, with nothing but a rope between them and the river.
scenes.caption: ROPES AND DYNAMITE
scenes.picture: A worker in a hardened cap swinging out from a cliff face on a rope, kicking off the rock with both feet, a pry bar in his hand, loose stones tumbling past.

scenes.narration: They soak cloth hats in tar until they harden. Hoover Dam is one of the first big projects to require hard hats, and when rocks rain down, those hats save lives.
scenes.caption: EARLY HARD HATS
scenes.picture: Close-up of a worker's hands holding a black tar-hardened cloth cap with a small dent in it, dusty overalls, soft daylight, blurred canyon behind.

scenes.narration: The official count is ninety-six deaths, though historians say heat and illness killed more. Every one of them was a husband, a son, or a father.
scenes.caption: 96 OFFICIAL DEATHS
scenes.picture: A quiet row of workers in caps holding them to their chests, heads bowed, standing at a canyon edge at sunset, long shadows over the desert.

scenes.narration: And there's one sad twist. The first man to die was a surveyor, J.G. Tierney, who drowned in 1922 searching for the dam site.
scenes.caption: THE TIERNEYS
scenes.picture: A lone 1920s surveyor in a hat and vest with a wooden tripod standing at a muddy river's edge in a canyon, water swirling around his boots, gray dawn.
scenes.era: Black Canyon on the Colorado River, 1922

scenes.narration: Thirteen years later to the day, his son Patrick fell from an intake tower, the last man to die on the dam.
scenes.caption: 13 YEARS LATER
scenes.picture: A tall concrete intake tower at dusk with a single hardened cloth cap lying on the platform edge, wind, long shadows, silent and sad mood.

scenes.narration: But the hardest problem isn't the river or the cliffs. It's the concrete.
scenes.caption: THE REAL ENEMY
scenes.picture: A wooden form filled with wet gray concrete, a worker in rubber boots standing beside it with arms crossed, looking thoughtful, a hand shovel leaning on the form, midday light.

scenes.narration: The dam needs more than three million cubic yards of it. Engineers said that's enough to pave a highway from San Francisco to New York.
scenes.caption: 3+ MILLION YARDS
scenes.picture: A gray two-lane highway stretching straight to the horizon across the American plains under a huge sky, a lone 1930s car driving on it, tiny in the distance.

scenes.narration: But concrete heats up as it hardens. Pour a block this big, and it would cook itself and crack.
scenes.caption: CONCRETE COOKS ITSELF
scenes.picture: A huge slab of fresh gray concrete with a jagged crack running through it and steam rising, a clean-shaven 1930s engineer in a brown felt hat kneeling beside it, alarmed.

scenes.narration: The engineers ran the numbers. Poured in one piece, it would take about a hundred and twenty-five years to cool.
scenes.caption: 125 YEARS
scenes.picture: A clean-shaven 1930s engineer in his 40s, white shirtsleeves and tie, brown felt hat, sitting at a drafting table with a pencil in hand, staring up in shock at a round wall clock.

scenes.narration: And a cracked dam, holding back a lake, would doom everything downstream.
scenes.caption: DISASTER RISK
scenes.picture: A dark stormy sky over a broken concrete wall with water gushing through a crack into a lower valley, tiny farmhouses and fields in danger below, dramatic.

scenes.narration: So they pour it in columns, like giant building blocks, letting each one cool before the next goes on top.
scenes.caption: BLOCK BY BLOCK
scenes.picture: Rows of tall square gray concrete columns rising side by side in a canyon like giant stepping blocks, workers with wooden forms on top, sunny day.

scenes.narration: Then comes the trick. Inside the blocks, they bury hundreds of miles of thin steel pipe.
scenes.caption: HIDDEN PIPES
scenes.picture: A tangle of thin steel pipes laid in neat coils across the top of a concrete block, a worker in a cap tightening a joint with a wrench, bright sunlight.

scenes.narration: Cold river water, then chilled water from a giant refrigeration plant, runs through the pipes and pulls the heat out.
scenes.caption: COOLING THE DAM
scenes.picture: A big 1930s industrial refrigeration plant with pipes and frosty tanks beside a canyon, cold mist drifting, two workers in caps checking dials.

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, giant buckets swing across the canyon on cables, dumping concrete into the forms.
scenes.caption: THE CABLEWAY
scenes.picture: A giant steel bucket of wet concrete hanging from thick cables high across a canyon, tilting to pour, tiny workers below, clear blue sky.

scenes.narration: Men stomp through the wet mix in heavy boots, packing it tight against the forms.
scenes.caption: BOOTS IN THE MIX
scenes.picture: Workers in tall rubber boots and cloth caps wading through wet gray concrete inside a wooden form, packing it tight with shovels, spattered faces.

scenes.narration: At night, floodlights make the canyon glow, and the pouring never stops.
scenes.caption: NIGHT SHIFT
scenes.picture: A night view of a canyon lit by bright floodlights, white concrete columns glowing, silhouettes of workers and a swinging cable bucket, starry sky.

scenes.narration: The wall climbs and curves upstream, so the weight of the lake will press it tighter into the rock.
scenes.caption: BUILT TO HOLD
scenes.picture: A partly built curved concrete dam wall seen from above in a canyon, its arc bending upstream toward a brown river, scaffolding and cables around it.

scenes.narration: But the clock is ticking. The deadline is 1938, with a heavy fine for every day they're late.
scenes.caption: THE DEADLINE
scenes.picture: A pocket watch lying open on a desk beside a large wall calendar fluttering in desert wind inside a drafting shack, tense low light, no readable writing.

scenes.narration: So Superintendent Frank Crowe pushes everyone hard. Men call him Hurry-Up Crowe, and the pace never lets up.
scenes.caption: HURRY-UP CROWE
scenes.picture: A stern middle-aged 1930s construction boss in a felt hat and rolled sleeves striding along a scaffold, pointing forward, workers hustling behind him.

scenes.narration: The men push too. In the worst years America has known, a paycheck is worth fighting for.
scenes.caption: WORTH FIGHTING FOR
scenes.picture: A tired smiling worker, about 30, short brown hair, dusty overalls, cloth cap, wiping sweat from his forehead beside a stack of wooden forms at sunset, pride on his face.

scenes.narration: And the last concrete is poured in 1935. The dam is done about two years ahead of schedule.
scenes.picture: Hundreds of workers in caps cheering and tossing their hats into the air on top of the finished huge concrete dam, bright blue sky, joyful faces.

scenes.narration: That September, President Franklin Roosevelt stands before the dam. "I came, I saw, and I was conquered," he says.
scenes.caption: THE DEDICATION
scenes.picture: President Franklin Roosevelt, smiling, dark suit and hat, seated in an open 1930s car on top of the dam, a blurred crowd of men and women in hats waving, sunny day.

scenes.narration: But the lights don't flip on that day. A year later, in 1936, the first power finally reaches Los Angeles.
scenes.caption: POWER ON
scenes.picture: Enormous steel generators humming in a long concrete power hall, one worker in overalls looking up in awe, glowing dials, bright overhead lamps.

scenes.narration: Lights come on across the Southwest, and cheap power and water help cities there grow.
scenes.caption: THE SOUTHWEST LIGHTS UP
scenes.picture: A small 1930s desert town at night with rows of glowing yellow windows and street lamps, electric poles marching across the dark plain, stars overhead.

scenes.narration: Behind the dam, a new lake spreads through the desert. It's Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the US by capacity.
scenes.caption: LAKE MEAD
scenes.picture: A vast blue lake stretching between red desert hills and brown cliffs under a pale sky, a small boat in the distance, quiet and wide shot.

scenes.narration: The dam tames the floods, and canals like the All-American Canal carry the river's water to the farms of the Imperial Valley.
scenes.caption: WATER FOR FARMS
scenes.picture: A straight irrigation canal with clear water running between green crop fields in a desert valley, a farmer in a straw hat smiling, 1930s.

scenes.narration: Some people say workers are buried inside the concrete. That's a myth. Records show no one is entombed in the dam.
scenes.caption: THE MYTH
scenes.picture: A thoughtful clean-shaven 1930s engineer in his 40s, white shirtsleeves, brown felt hat, resting one hand on a smooth solid concrete wall, shaking his head with a small smile, warm light.

scenes.narration: Today, Lake Mead still supplies water to tens of millions of people, and the dam still generates power for the Southwest.
scenes.caption: STILL WORKING
scenes.picture: The finished Hoover Dam in golden evening light, water flowing from the powerhouse at its foot into the canyon, calm blue lake behind it, wide shot.

scenes.narration: When a country has nothing left but its people, it turns out that can be enough to hold back a river.
scenes.caption: THE ANSWER
scenes.picture: A lean worker, about 30, short brown hair, dusty overalls, cloth cap, sitting on a concrete ledge at sunset looking out over the dam and calm lake below, peaceful tired smile, golden light.

narrator: Epic historical narrator, deep and confident, dramatic swells, quick through action, slower only for the final line.

short.title: How Jobless Men Built Hoover Dam
short.description:
In 1931, broke Americans moved a river and cooled a mountain of concrete to build Hoover Dam. Here's how they did it.
The true story of the Hoover Dam in under a minute.

scenes.narration: In 1931, thousands of jobless Americans went into a desert canyon to build Hoover Dam.
scenes.caption: HOOVER DAM, 1931
scenes.picture: A sweating American construction worker, about 30, lean build, short dark hair, dirty overalls and gray cloth cap, face large and central, determined eyes, a huge half-built concrete dam wall rising behind him in a Nevada desert canyon, orange evening light, 1931.

scenes.narration: Their problem: a concrete wall so big it would crack itself as it hardened.
scenes.caption: IT COULD CRACK
scenes.picture: A giant slab of fresh gray concrete with a jagged crack running across it and steam rising from the surface, a worried 1930s engineer in a brown hat and white shirt crouching beside it, staring at the crack, desert canyon behind.

scenes.narration: And first, they had to move the wild Colorado River out of the way.
scenes.caption: THE QUESTION
scenes.picture: A rushing brown Colorado River twisting through a red rock Black Canyon, a determined 1930s worker, about 30, lean, dark hair, gray cloth cap and overalls, standing large at the river edge, hands on hips, looking at the water.

scenes.narration: America was broke, and millions of men needed work.
scenes.caption: AMERICA, 1931
scenes.picture: Three thin 1930s American men in worn flat caps and patched jackets, tired hollow faces, standing in a line on a dusty street in front of a closed brick factory with broken windows, gray Depression sky.

scenes.narration: Then word spread of a giant dam on the Colorado River.
scenes.caption: A GIANT DAM
scenes.picture: Two hopeful young men in worn 1930s clothes, bundles on their backs, clinging to the open door of a steam freight train boxcar speeding through the Nevada desert at sunrise, wind in their hair, smiling.

scenes.narration: But summer heat hit a hundred and twenty degrees.
scenes.caption: 120 DEGREES
scenes.picture: A blazing white sun over a dusty desert work camp of canvas tents, in the foreground an exhausted 1930s worker, about 30, lean, dark hair, gray cloth cap, wiping sweat from his forehead with a rag, heat haze shimmering.

scenes.narration: So crews blasted four giant tunnels to move the river.
scenes.caption: FOUR TUNNELS
scenes.picture: A huge round tunnel mouth blasted into a red canyon wall, brown Colorado River water pouring into it, a 1930s worker, about 30, lean, gray cloth cap and overalls, standing large in the foreground watching, dust in the air.

scenes.narration: In one piece, the concrete would take a hundred and twenty-five years to cool.
scenes.caption: 125 YEARS
scenes.picture: A stunned clean-shaven 1930s engineer in shirtsleeves, suspenders and a hat, sitting at a wooden drafting table with rolled blueprints, staring up at a round wall clock, eyes wide, close-up of face in an office.

scenes.narration: So engineers poured it in columns, like giant building blocks.
scenes.caption: BLOCK BY BLOCK
scenes.picture: Tall square gray concrete columns rising side by side in a canyon like giant stepping blocks, two 1930s workers in caps setting wooden forms on top of one column, sunny day, steel cable crane above.

scenes.narration: Hundreds of miles of cold-water pipes pulled out the heat.
scenes.caption: HIDDEN PIPES
scenes.picture: A tangle of thin steel pipes coiled across the top of a fresh concrete block, a 1930s worker in a cap tightening a pipe joint with a big wrench, cool mist rising from the pipe, bright sunlight, close-up of hands and pipes.

scenes.narration: Working day and night, the men finished two years early.
scenes.caption: TWO YEARS EARLY
scenes.picture: A cheering crowd of 1930s workers in caps and overalls throwing their hats into the blue sky on top of a finished concrete dam, joyful open-mouthed faces, two smiling men large in the foreground, bright sunny day.

scenes.narration: Jobless men beat the river and the heat, and the dam still powers the Southwest.
scenes.caption: THE ANSWER
scenes.picture: The finished Hoover Dam, a huge curved concrete wall, glowing in golden evening light above a calm blue lake, a lone worker, about 30, lean, dark hair, gray cloth cap and overalls, sitting large in the foreground, peaceful smile, seen from behind-side.
